standard.title: Target language and English similarities and differences
standard.description: notice that the target language has features that may be similar to or different from English
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have noticed some similarities and differences between target language and English sounds and features with support (AC9LSF02). They are developing early English literacy. They have not yet systematically compared structural features across the two languages.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students notice and describe features of the target language that are similar to or different from English — including structural patterns, shared vocabulary, text conventions and written features — drawing on both languages as reference points.

nodes.label: Shared vocabulary and structural comparisons
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify vocabulary shared across the target language and English, and notice structural patterns that are similar to or different from English.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three shared target language-English vocabulary items and explain what makes them recognisable; identify at least one structural difference between the two languages.
nodes.typical_width: Notice and collect shared vocabulary across the two languages; notice structural patterns — including word order, grammatical categories — that are similar to or different from English; compare how sentences are built differently; create bilingual comparison resources.
wider: Find shared vocabulary items independently and test whether their meaning is truly equivalent — identify any that appear similar but mean something different
Compare a familiar target language text with its English equivalent — list every structural difference noticed
nodes.hinge_reason: Using English as a reference point for target language structure is a productive metalinguistic strategy that accelerates grammatical awareness. Students who make these comparisons explicitly build transferable understanding; students who treat the two languages as completely separate miss the scaffolding that comparison provides.

response_modes.reason: Cross-language comparison requires holding both languages in mind simultaneously and describing the relationship. Structured comparison tasks — side-by-side sentence pairs, bilingual charts — scaffold this dual-language attention.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three shared target language-English vocabulary items and explains what makes them recognisable
Identifies at least one structural difference between the target language and English with a supporting example

nodes.label: Text features and vocabulary borrowing across languages
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notice similarities and differences in text features across the target language and English — including text type conventions, written features and borrowed vocabulary.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one text feature that differs between target language and English texts and explain the difference; identify at least one example of vocabulary borrowing between the two languages.
nodes.typical_width: Compare text type conventions across the target language and English (e.g. story openings, greeting card language); compare written features (punctuation, capitalisation); identify vocabulary borrowed between the two languages; create identity texts with parallel information in both languages.
wider: Find examples of words borrowed from the target language into English and from English into the target language — explain what the borrowing pattern reveals about how languages influence each other
Compare a familiar target language text type with its English equivalent — annotate every difference noticed

response_modes.reason: Cross-language noticing develops most richly through varied comparison contexts — text types, word types, borrowings. Each new context reveals a different dimension of the language relationship.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Noticing vocabulary borrowing in both directions positions language learning as part of a broader story of how languages influence each other — building genuine linguistic curiosity.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one text feature that differs between target language and English and explains the difference
Identifies at least two borrowed vocabulary items and explains what they show about language contact
